memoryText: You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Isaiah 26:3 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This promise comes in the middle of Isaiah’s apocalypse, a section about the shaking of the whole earth. It is a song of confidence for the day of salvation, sung in a time of upheaval. Peace is promised, and it is promised in the midst of unrest.

“You keep him in perfect peace.” In Hebrew, the words are “peace, peace,” shalom shalom. The double word indicates fullness, a peace that is complete. It is not the absence of trouble but wholeness: well-being in body, soul, and relationships. And the one who gives it is God. He keeps, or guards, the person. The word is used of a sentry on watch.

“Whose mind is stayed on you.” The word “stayed” means supported, leaning, resting on something. The mind that is steadied by God is a mind that is propped up. It is a picture of leaning on God, as one leans on a strong staff. The mind in view is not only intellect but the whole inner life, our thoughts, imaginings, and desires. When the center of our attention is God, the heart is stable.

“Because he trusts in you.” The ground of the peace is trust. The man in this verse is not free of problems. He is anchored. Isaiah’s contrast is clear throughout this week’s reading: the people of Judah were anxious because they trusted in Egypt, in treaties, and in horses. The peace came to those who trusted in the LORD, like Hezekiah on the day he spread the letter before him.

Say this verse in times of worry and ask what you are leaning on. In Christ, the Prince of Peace has made peace for us through his blood. He now says, “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you.”
weekInReview: This week you read the middle chapters of Isaiah’s first half. You prayed Psalm 83 against a coalition of enemy nations and saw that the real aim is that they would know the LORD is the Most High. You read the Isaiah Apocalypse, with its picture of a feast on God’s mountain, the swallowing up of death, and the promise of resurrection. You read the woes against trusting in Egypt, and the beautiful invitation to “return and rest.” You saw the cornerstone laid in Zion and heard of the Way of Holiness. Then you followed the Assyrian crisis through Isaiah’s eyes: Hezekiah spreading the letter before the LORD, the angel striking the camp, and the king’s illness, his healing, and his misstep with Babylon. The week taught that peace belongs to the mind that is stayed on God, and that those who trust in worldly power will be disappointed.
reflectionQuestions: Isaiah calls us to “quietness and trust” rather than frantic human schemes. Where do you need to stop striving and rest in God?
Isaiah 25:8 promises that God will swallow up death forever and wipe away tears. How does this promise speak to your own grief or fear?
Hezekiah faithfully prayed in a crisis but was careless in success. In what area of your life is prosperity a bigger test than trouble?
prayerPrompts: Ask God to keep you in perfect peace with your mind stayed on him.
Thank Christ for swallowing up death in victory.
